Figure 1:Action as world coordinates.(a) In a planar-camera world, each action corresponds to a known translation of the scene.
(b) Standard RoPE re-addresses the same scene token after the camera moves, while ActionRoPE adds the camera displacement to each token’s position, keeping its index across frames.
(c) ActionRoPE enables precise motion and revisits, control in unseen scenes, and variable camera speed, without adding parameters to the control path.

Figure 2:Overview of ActionRoPE.The left panel shows the video DiT, where ActionRoPE replaces the screen-relative RoPE before self-attention and the known/new maskκ\kappais added to the patch embedding through a zero-initialized convolution. By binding camera motion to world coordinates, ActionRoPE keeps the same positional index for the same scene location across views, as illustrated in the upper-right panel. The same coordinates reveal which regions are known or newly revealed, and CNS assigns them different denoising schedules, as shown in the lower-right panel.

Figure 3:Qualitative comparison of revisit consistency.For each scene, the leftmost column shows the first frame. For each method, the top row shows the final frame after a full round trip, and the bottom row shows its absolute error against the first frame (blue indicates low and red indicates high error). Our method keeps the error low across the whole scene, while the four baselines show clearly larger errors that come from shifted or regenerated content.

Figure 4:Control on out-of-distribution first frames.Each row starts from a first frame in a visual style that is absent from the training game (watercolor and bamboo forest, respectively), and the columns show the generated frames at increasing frame indexff.

Figure 5:Control on different backbones.The same first frame and command are given to ActionRoPE on SkyReels-V2, LTX-2.5 and MiniMax-H3. The camera moves right and turns back atf=40f=40, and the columns show frames at increasing time.
Figure 6:More revisit comparisons (I).For each scene, we show the final frame of each method after the round trip and its error map against the first frame.
Figure 7:More revisit comparisons (II).Same layout as Figure6, on three other evaluation scenes.

Figure 8:Measured versus commanded displacement.Each point is one clip, the orange line connects the medians at each speed, and the dashed line marks exact tracking. The slope andR2R^{2}are those of Table1.
Figure 9:Revisit comparison on out-of-distribution scenes.The three first frames show an arctic tundra, a medieval castle and an underwater ruin. Same layout as Figure6.
Figure 10:More out-of-distribution styles.Our method on four first frames with styles that never appear in the training game, under a command that moves right and turns back atf=40f{=}40.
Figure 11:Cross-backbone example (I).The same first frame and command on the four backbones.
Figure 12:Cross-backbone example (II).Same setting as Figure11, on another evaluation scene.

Figure 13:Sampling with and without CNS.Clean-frame estimates of the last frame during sampling, under a straight walk to the right. The region to the left of the orange line is covered by the first frame.
Figure 14:Revisit with and without CNS.Final frames after the round trip and their error maps, for our full model and the model trained without CNS.
